summary: Clarifies the zero window probes described in RFC 1122, which a TCP sender uses when the receiver says it has no room. It explains that what had been done by some implementations came from a misinterpretation. It is informational, and it was replaced by RFC 9293.

eli5.summary: If a friend says their hands are full, you keep asking every so often whether they have a free hand. This clears up how long and how to keep asking, and it was later replaced by RFC 9293.

questions: what is tcp zero window probe
why does tcp keep probing a zero window
what is the tcp persist condition
how does zero window probing prevent connection hang
subtitle: When the receiver has no room, the sender keeps checking if that changes.

tldr.problem: When a TCP receiver's window closes to zero, the sender cannot send. If acknowledgments that reopen the window are lost, the connection could hang forever.
tldr.mechanism: The sender periodically probes with zero-window probes (ZWPs) to detect when the receiver has room again, and must not close the connection just because it is stuck in this persist condition.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6429 clarifies RFC 1122 by requiring that connections in persist state stay open, but also permitting applications and operating systems to close them to prevent denial-of-service attacks.

today: RFC 6429 was obsoleted by RFC 9293, a consolidated TCP specification. The principles clarified in RFC 6429 are now part of RFC 9293.

sections.title: Introduction and the Persist Condition
sections.content:
RFC 1122 specifies that a TCP sender must support zero-window probes (ZWPs): periodic probe packets sent when a receiver advertises a receive window of zero. This condition, called the persist condition, can arise when a receiver's application is not reading data, for example a printer waiting for paper to be reloaded. The sender must allow the connection to stay open and keep probing, because when the receiver has room again, its acknowledgments might confirm the data can be sent.

However, some TCP implementations misinterpreted RFC 1122 to mean that connections in persist state must never be closed, creating a security vulnerability.
sections.eli5: When a receiver says it has no space, the sender asks every so often if space is available. The connection should stay open because space might come back soon, like a printer waiting for paper.

sections.title: How the Persist Condition Works
sections.content:
In normal TCP operation, a receiver advertises a receive window that tells the sender how many bytes it can accept. The sender uses this window to control how much data it sends. When a receiver closes its window to zero, the sender enters the persist condition and stops sending data. Instead, it sends zero-window probes at intervals to test if the window has reopened. As long as the receiver sends acknowledgments of these probes, the connection can remain in this state indefinitely.

This behaviour is intentional: an application might legitimately block on reading from a connection for hours or days, and the TCP layer should not forcibly close it. For example, a user might pause a large file download while multitasking, and the connection should be available when the user resumes.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps sending tiny probe packets that say "Do you have space yet?" The receiver answers "No." This can go on for hours, and that is fine because the receiver might eventually read the data.

sections.title: The Denial-of-Service Risk
sections.content:
The vulnerability arises when an attacker exploits the persist condition to exhaust server resources. A malicious client can open a connection to a server, send a request, and then deliberately stop reading the response. The client's TCP then advertises a zero window, forcing the server to hold the response data in its send buffer and enter persist condition. If an attacker opens many such connections, the server's kernel memory for TCP buffers becomes exhausted, preventing legitimate connections from being established or served.

The RFC notes that orphaned connections (where the application has closed the socket but the TCP connection remains) are particularly problematic because no process monitors them for resource management. A CERT advisory documented this attack scenario.
sections.eli5: An attacker can open many connections and deliberately refuse to read the responses. The server has to keep the data, hogging memory. With enough fake connections, legitimate users cannot connect anymore.

sections.title: Clarification of RFC 1122 Requirement
sections.content:
RFC 6429 clarifies that RFC 1122 requires TCP implementations to NOT close a connection merely because it is stuck in persist condition. However, the document adds an implicit requirement: TCP must allow applications and operating system resource managers to close or abort such connections. This can be done through application-level interfaces or administrative mechanisms, without violating RFC 1122.

The clarification is that persistence in zero-window-probe mode is not an excuse for TCP to ignore application requests to close the connection. Operating systems should provide mechanisms to reclaim resources from connections that are not making progress, protecting against the denial-of-service scenario described above.
sections.eli5: A connection can stay stuck waiting for the receiver to have space, but the application or system administrator must be able to force it closed if needed. This stops attackers from filling up all the server's memory with stuck connections.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 6429 is an informational document that clarifies the RFC 1122 behaviour, not a change to the standard. It was made obsolete by RFC 9293, which provides a consolidated TCP specification. The principles of the persist condition and the need for resource management continue to apply in modern TCP implementations.
sections.eli5: This document was replaced by a newer, complete TCP specification (RFC 9293) that includes these same ideas.
